reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: An infiltrative disorder in which misfolded protein deposits stiffen the myocardium, producing a restrictive cardiomyopathy and heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
The two dominant cardiac types are AL amyloidosis from immunoglobulin light chains and transthyretin (ATTR) amyloidosis, which may be hereditary or age-related wild-type
A discrepancy between marked left ventricular wall thickening on echocardiography and low voltages on the ECG is a classic clue
Associated features may include carpal tunnel syndrome, spinal stenosis, and unexplained neuropathy, sometimes preceding cardiac disease by years
Bone scintigraphy tracers avidly localise to ATTR deposits, allowing non-biopsy diagnosis once a monoclonal protein has been excluded
Cardiac MRI shows characteristic diffuse late gadolinium enhancement and abnormal tissue mapping
Patients are often sensitive to and intolerant of standard heart failure and rate-controlling drugs because of the restrictive physiology
Distinguishing AL from ATTR is essential because treatment and prognosis differ substantially
reference.pathophysiology: Cardiac amyloidosis results from extracellular deposition of insoluble amyloid fibrils within the myocardial interstitium. In AL disease the fibrils derive from clonal immunoglobulin light chains produced by a plasma cell disorder, whereas in ATTR disease they arise from destabilised transthyretin, either due to inherited mutations or age-related wild-type misfolding. Amyloid infiltration increases wall thickness and stiffness, impairing diastolic filling and producing restrictive physiology; conduction tissue and small vessels may also be affected, and in AL disease light chains exert additional direct myocardial toxicity.
additionalDifferentials: Other restrictive cardiomyopathies including endomyocardial fibrosis
Cardiac sarcoidosis and other infiltrative diseases
additionalInvestigations: Echocardiography for wall thickening, restrictive filling, and reduced longitudinal strain with apical sparing
ECG for low voltages and conduction abnormalities
Serum and urine tests for monoclonal light chains, including free light chain assay
Bone scintigraphy for ATTR amyloid uptake
Cardiac MRI with mapping and late gadolinium enhancement
Tissue biopsy with amyloid typing when the diagnosis remains uncertain
Genetic testing to distinguish hereditary from wild-type ATTR
redFlags: Progressive heart failure with hypotension and poor drug tolerance
Ventricular arrhythmia or evidence of sudden death risk
Rapid clinical deterioration suggesting AL amyloidosis with a plasma cell dyscrasia
reference.prognosis: Untreated AL cardiac amyloidosis carries a particularly poor prognosis, whereas ATTR forms progress more slowly; earlier diagnosis and disease-modifying therapy have improved outcomes. Overall prognosis is driven by the amyloid type, the degree of cardiac involvement reflected in biomarkers, and the presence of arrhythmia or advanced heart failure.
pitfalls: Mislabelling amyloid wall thickening as hypertensive or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Interpreting a positive bone scan as ATTR without excluding a monoclonal protein
Precipitating hypotension with aggressive diuresis, beta-blockade, or vasodilators
Overlooking systemic clues such as carpal tunnel syndrome or neuropathy
Delaying referral for AL disease, where prompt haematological treatment is time-critical
